newsitem.title: USA: No U.S. decision on certifying Mexico until Friday.
newsitem.headline: No U.S. decision on certifying Mexico until Friday.

text.p: The Clinton administration will not decide whether to certify Mexico as an ally in the drug war until Friday at the earliest, the State Department said on Wednesday amid new congressional calls to get tough.

"The announcement will definitely not be tomorrow because I know the secretary of state has to have a meeting with her advisers and then she needs to make a formal recommendation to the president and then they need to sit down with him," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright must make a recommendation to President Bill Clinton on whether to grant certification to Mexico and 31 other countries as partners in the international battle against illegal drugs. Countries that fail this test face possible economic sanctions.

The decision is officially due on Saturday but Burns indicated this might not be a firm deadline. "I haven't consulted a lawyer to know if it has to be by midnight or Friday or whether it could be Saturday or Sunday or Monday," he said. "That's a question for the lawyers."

Mexico has passed this annual test since 1986, when Congress mandated that the White House certify whether major drug producing or transit countries were cooperating with U.S. anti-narcotics efforts. But the dismissal last week of Mexico's drug czar Gen. Jesus Gutierrez amid charges that he was on the payroll of a drug baron sparked calls in Washington for tough action against the Mexican government.

Sen. Phil Gramm, a Texas Republican, on Wednesday added his voice to the congressional chorus calling for a change in the U.S. policy toward Mexico. Noting that he routinely had favoured certification for Mexico in the past, Gramm said in a statement:

"Mexico is a neighbour and one of our largest trading partners, but I do not believe that we can continue to close our eyes to the common corruption of Mexican officials which permits the drug cartels to poison America's youth."

Other lawmakers who have spoken out against certification for Mexico include Democratic Sens. Joseph Biden of Delaware, Dianne Feinstein of California and Robert Torricelli of New Jersey and House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt, a Missouri Democrat.

Without hinting which way Albright was leaning, Burns said that given the "very surprising and dramatic and even tragic announcements out of Mexico" the U.S. reaction should not be to isolate Mexico. "It should be to work with Mexico," Burns said.
